items.followUp: Explain why atomic radius generally decreases across a period.

rubric.why: Identifies the increase in nuclear attraction across a period.
rubric.description: Nuclear charge or effective nuclear charge increases across a period.
rubric.how: Award for stating that increasing nuclear charge attracts the electrons more strongly.

rubric.why: Connects the stronger attraction to the energy needed to remove an electron.
rubric.description: Electrons are held more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove one.
rubric.how: Award for linking stronger attraction to the increase in ionization energy.

modelAnswer: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell.
The stronger attraction holds the outer electrons more tightly, so more energy is needed to remove one.

items.followUp: In a coordinate covalent bond, what is the role of a donor atom?

rubric.why: States what the donor contributes to the coordinate covalent bond.
rubric.description: A donor atom provides a lone pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award for identifying donation of a lone pair or electron pair.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the acceptor by what it receives.
rubric.description: An acceptor atom accepts the donated pair, usually into a vacant orbital.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the acceptor receives the donated electron pair.

modelAnswer: A donor atom provides a lone pair of electrons to form a coordinate covalent bond.
An acceptor atom receives this pair, usually into a vacant orbital.

items.followUp: What type of atoms commonly form hydrogen bonds? Give one example of a substance that shows hydrogen bonding.

rubric.why: Identifies the atoms involved in hydrogen bonding.
rubric.description: Hydrogen bonding is an attraction involving hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as F, O or N.
rubric.how: Award for describing the attraction involving hydrogen attached to F, O or N.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of hydrogen bonding.
rubric.description: Gives an example, such as water or hydrogen fluoride.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is the attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
Example: hydrogen bonding between water molecules.

items.followUp: State two properties of ionic compounds.

rubric.why: Identifies a typical physical property of covalent compounds.
rubric.description: Covalent compounds generally have low melting or boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for stating either low melting point or low boiling point.

rubric.why: Identifies another typical physical property of covalent compounds.
rubric.description: Covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Award for stating that covalent compounds are poor or non-conductors of electricity.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
They are generally poor conductors of electricity.

items.followUp: What happens to the forward and reverse reaction rates at dynamic equilibrium?

rubric.why: States the defining rate condition for dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: The forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the two reaction rates become equal.

rubric.why: Explains why equilibrium is dynamic while observable amounts remain unchanged.
rubric.description: Both reactions continue, while the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
rubric.how: Award for stating that concentrations remain constant or that both reactions continue.

modelAnswer: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction in a closed system when the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
Both reactions continue, but the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and state what change of state occurs at the freezing point.

rubric.why: Identifies the change of state at boiling.
rubric.description: At the boiling point, a liquid changes into a gas or vapour.
rubric.how: Award for correctly describing liquid changing to gas or vapour.

rubric.why: Identifies the change of state at freezing.
rubric.description: At the freezing point, a liquid changes into a solid.
rubric.how: Award for correctly describing liquid changing to solid.

modelAnswer: The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas.
The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a solid.

items.followUp: What is the transition temperature of sulphur, and what change occurs at this temperature?

rubric.why: Defines the change associated with a transition temperature.
rubric.description: It is the temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another.
rubric.how: Award for describing the change from one allotropic form to another.

rubric.why: Gives the transition temperature of sulphur.

modelAnswer: Transition temperature is the temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another.
The transition temperature of sulphur is about 95.5 °C.

items.followUp: Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 0.5 mol of solute in 2 dm³ of solution.

rubric.why: Defines molarity using the amount of solute and the volume of solution.
rubric.description: Molarity is the number of moles of solute per dm³ (litre) of solution.
rubric.how: Award for the correct definition, with volume referring to the solution.

rubric.why: Gives the standard symbol for molarity.
rubric.how: Award for writing the symbol M.

modelAnswer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved in one dm³ (one litre) of solution.
